title: Industrial Union Department, AFL-CIO v. American Petroleum Institute (1980) (the Benzene Case)
shortTitle: Industrial Union Department, AFL-CIO v. American Petroleum Institute (1980) — the Benzene Case
summary: Before OSHA sets a permanent health standard for a toxic substance it must find that the existing exposure level poses a significant risk of harm that the new standard would reduce.
notes:
Key line: "But 'safe' is not the equivalent of 'risk-free.'" Justice Stevens, announcing the judgment of the Court.

Citation: 448 U.S. 607 (1980).

sections.Parties: Petitioners were the Industrial Union Department of the AFL-CIO, a labor federation representing workers exposed to benzene, and Ray Marshall, Secretary of Labor, whose Occupational Safety and Health Administration issued the standard. Respondents were the American Petroleum Institute and other industry groups, including rubber manufacturers and chemical companies, whose members would have had to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to comply. The union and the Secretary defended the standard as required by the Act's mandate to protect workers from toxic substances. The industry argued that OSHA had not shown the standard was reasonably necessary or supported by substantial evidence.
sections.Material Facts: Benzene is a chemical used in making motor fuels, solvents, detergents and pesticides, and exposure at high levels causes leukemia and blood disorders. The existing consensus standard, adopted in 1971, limited airborne benzene to 10 parts per million averaged over eight hours. In 1977 OSHA adopted a carcinogen policy that no safe level of exposure could be determined and that exposure limits for carcinogens should be set at the lowest technologically feasible level. On February 10, 1978, OSHA issued a permanent standard reducing the limit to 1 ppm and banning dermal contact with liquid benzene. OSHA estimated compliance would require about $266 million in capital investment, first-year costs of $187 million to $205 million and recurring annual costs of about $34 million, to reduce exposure for roughly 35,000 workers. OSHA made no finding that exposure at 10 ppm had caused leukemia.
sections.Procedural History: Industry groups petitioned for pre-enforcement review in the Fifth Circuit. That court held the standard invalid in 1978, finding that OSHA had not shown by substantial evidence that the benefits of the 1 ppm limit bore a reasonable relationship to its costs and that the dermal contact ban lacked support. The union and the Secretary sought certiorari. The Supreme Court heard argument on October 10, 1979, and affirmed on July 2, 1980, with no opinion commanding a majority.
sections.Issue: Section 6(b)(5) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act tells the Secretary to set the standard that most adequately assures, to the extent feasible, that no employee suffers material impairment of health, while section 3(8) defines a standard as one reasonably necessary or appropriate to provide safe employment. OSHA read the first provision to require the lowest feasible exposure limit for carcinogens. Did the Act authorize OSHA to reduce the permissible exposure limit for benzene from 10 ppm to 1 ppm without first finding that exposure at the existing level posed a significant risk of material health impairment?
sections.Holding: No. Section 3(8) of the Act, which defines a standard as one reasonably necessary or appropriate to provide safe or healthful employment, requires OSHA to make a threshold finding that the workplace is unsafe in the sense that significant risks are present and can be reduced. Safe does not mean risk-free. OSHA relied on its carcinogen policy and assumptions rather than findings, so the standard was invalid. The Fifth Circuit's judgment was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Stevens wrote for a plurality. He read section 3(8) into section 6(b)(5), so that even a standard for toxic materials must first be reasonably necessary to remedy a significant risk; otherwise the Act would give OSHA power to impose enormous costs to achieve trivial gains, a sweeping delegation that Congress did not make and that would raise nondelegation concerns. Legislative history showed Congress aimed at eliminating significant harm rather than all risk. OSHA bore the burden of showing, on substantial evidence, that it is more likely than not that long-term exposure at 10 ppm presents a significant risk. The plurality stressed that the requirement is not a mathematical straitjacket: OSHA may use conservative assumptions and need not wait for deaths, but it must make some rational judgment about the magnitude of risk. Here OSHA had instead shifted the burden to industry to prove a safe level existed. The dermal contact ban failed for the same reason. Justice Powell, concurring in part, would also require OSHA to show that costs bear a reasonable relationship to benefits. Justice Rehnquist would have held section 6(b)(5) an unconstitutional delegation because the phrase to the extent feasible gives the Secretary no guidance on where to set a standard when no safe level is known.

topics.lrs-i-major-questions: The note treats Benzene’s demand for a clearer mandate for sweeping authority as a precursor to major-questions reasoning.
topics.lrs-i-major-questions-rationales: The plurality’s avoidance rationale and Rehnquist’s direct constitutional position illustrate different judicial responses to broad delegation.
topics.lrs-i-risk-assessment: The accompanying notes explain the scientific and policy judgments required by significant-risk assessment.

learning.separateOpinions: The judgment was 5 to 4. Justice Stevens announced the judgment in an opinion joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Stewart, and by Justice Powell in part. Chief Justice Burger concurred briefly. Justice Powell concurred in part and in the judgment, adding a cost-benefit requirement. Justice Rehnquist concurred in the judgment on nondelegation grounds. Justice Marshall dissented, joined by Justices Brennan, White and Blackmun, arguing that the plain text of section 6(b)(5) required the standard that most adequately assures no material impairment to the extent feasible, that OSHA's findings were supported by substantial evidence, and that the plurality substituted its own regulatory policy for that of Congress.
